title: Optimized banana leaf ash concrete: Mechanical performance, durability, and sustainability assessment
content:
Abstract

The production of Portland cement contributes significantly to global carbon emissions, which has increased the interest in agricultural waste-based supplementary cementitious materials. This study investigated banana leaf ash (BLA) as a partial cement replacement and evaluated its influence on the mechanical behavior, durability, and sustainability performance of concrete. Four concrete mixes containing 0%, 5%, 10%, and 15% BLA were tested for compressive, split tensile, and flexural strengths at 7, 14, and 28 days. The results demonstrated that concrete incorporating 10% BLA achieved the most favorable mechanical performance, showing enhanced compressive strength at 28 days compared to the control mix and other replacement levels. Lower replacement levels (5% BLA) exhibited marginal strength improvement, whereas higher replacement levels (15% BLA) resulted in a reduction in strength due to the dilution of cementitious compounds and reduced hydration efficiency. The split tensile and flexural strengths followed a similar trend, with peak values observed at 10% BLA replacement. Water absorption decreased consistently with increasing BLA content, indicating improved pore refinement, although workability was reduced because of the angular and porous nature of the ash. Embodied energy and cost analyses showed measurable reductions in material cost and energy demand with increasing BLA content. The life cycle assessment indicates the potential for lowering CO2 emissions, primarily through reduced cement consumption. BLA can serve as a viable partial cement replacement, with 10% providing the most balanced improvement in mechanical performance, durability, and environmental benefits.
